tagline.text: A hidden jungle waterfall and cool natural pool near Port Barton

location.label: Location
location.text: Pamuayan, Port Barton, San Vicente, Palawan

children.text: Pamuayan Falls is an eight-meter waterfall hidden in the jungle behind Port Barton, Palawan. It runs on voluntary donations instead of an entrance fee, and its small natural pool is perfect for a swim and a rest, adding a refreshing change to a beach-focused Port Barton itinerary.

Pamuayan Falls lies in the jungle of Pamuayan, an inland area reached from Port Barton, a small village in the municipality of San Vicente on Palawan's west coast. Locals also call it Papawyan Falls. At about
8m
high, it is not a towering cascade, but the dense forest, the stream and the rocks around it create a cozy, intimate atmosphere.

Unlike El Nido or Coron, Port Barton still has the feel of a quiet backpacker village, so most travelers enjoy the sea on island-hopping tours and set aside a day for an inland trip to this waterfall. Port Barton is a small coastal village in San Vicente, about
3–4 hours

overland from Puerto Princesa. Guesthouses and restaurants line the beach, and island-hopping tours are the main activity. That makes the falls a good side trip: block out half a day between your sea outings. Rather than expecting a grand attraction with facilities, think of it as a quiet forest walk ending in a cold plunge, and you will likely be very happy with it.
At the entrance there is a small checkpoint and a logbook. There is no fixed entrance fee and the site is run on voluntary donations. Visitors are said to put about
in the donation box. The money goes toward maintaining the trail and facilities, so it is good manners to give even a small amount. Many reviews say there is no pushy mandatory guide fee.
The road includes unpaved sections and turns muddy in the rain. On foot it takes about
1.5–2 hours
from the village; by tricycle or motorbike you can reach the area near the entrance in about
15–20 minutes
. Either way, the last stretch is a walk of about
15 minutes
through the forest.

blocks.title: An eight-meter waterfall in the jungle

children.text: Water drops from about
8m
high through dense forest. It is a small waterfall rather than a big one, but with few visitors it is a good place to enjoy in quiet.

blocks.title: A natural pool below the falls

children.text: A small pool below the falls is good for swimming. The water is cold and refreshing, ideal after a sweaty walk. The pool is not large, though, so it can feel cramped when crowds arrive; going on a quiet morning is better.

blocks.title: A forest trail across the stream

children.text: From the entrance checkpoint to the falls you walk about
15 minutes

over stepping stones and along the stream. The path is fairly clear, but the rocks by the water are slippery. If you have already worked up a sweat on the way from town, the shaded last stretch of forest is a welcome relief.

At the entrance you write your name in the logbook and give whatever you wish to the donation box. With no fixed fee, it is easy on the budget. The donations go toward maintaining the trail and facilities, so giving what you can is the way to keep enjoying this waterfall for years to come.
Near the falls there is a small hut where you can leave your bag and clothes and rest. It comes in handy when you need a place for your things while swimming.

blocks.title: A scenic ride through village life

children.text: The way from Port Barton to the falls passes country villages, fields and coconut groves, so the trip itself becomes part of the sightseeing. You can see everyday village life along the road, so take your time and enjoy the scenery as you go.
Pamuayan Beach is included in some island-hopping routes, and one guide says the falls are only a few minutes' walk from that beach. Matching your trip with a hopping tour is another option.

Have breakfast in Port Barton village and pack water, a towel, a change of clothes and cash. Negotiate a round-trip fare with waiting time in advance with your accommodation or a village tricycle driver.
Set off by tricycle or motorbike. There are unpaved sections, so it takes about
15–20 minutes
Sign the logbook at the entrance checkpoint and put about
in the donation box.
Walk the forest trail for about
15 minutes
to reach the falls. Be careful not to slip when crossing the stepping stones.
Swim in the pool below the falls, rest and take photos. The morning, when few people are around, is quiet and pleasant.
Return the same way and have lunch at a restaurant in the village. In the afternoon, relax on the beach or book an island-hopping tour for the next day to keep your plans running smoothly.
A morning trip lets you avoid the midday heat and afternoon showers. On rainy days the road turns to mud, so it is better to postpone.

children.text: Leave Port Barton village before the sun gets hot. The walk takes about
1.5–2 hours
one way, so bring plenty of water.
Arrive at the entrance checkpoint, sign the logbook and make a donation.
Walk about
15 minutes
through the forest to reach the falls and swim.
The way back may include uphill sections and mud, so save your energy and move slowly.

Walking distances feel different to everyone. If you are sensitive to heat or short on time, you can ride one way. When you walk, your energy tends to drop on the way back, so it is best not to plan anything strenuous for the afternoon.

items.title: From the village to the falls

children.text: A tricycle costs about
for a round trip with waiting time (it varies with group size and bargaining).
A motorbike rental costs about
per day. A semi-automatic bike is recommended because of the muddy roads.
On foot, it takes about
1.5–2 hours
one way.
From the entrance, you always have to walk about
15 minutes

The dry season from December to May is the best time to go. The road is dry and the water is clear, making trekking and swimming easy. December to February is peak season, so all of Port Barton is crowded and rooms fill up quickly.

In the rainy season the unpaved road turns to mud and the stream can swell and become dangerous. Avoid going right after heavy rain. Within a day, the cooler, quieter morning is best. When the water level drops the stream can become thin, so for a fuller waterfall the ideal time is just after moderate rain, once the road has dried.

Most visitors stay in Port Barton village. There are backpacker guesthouses, beachfront cottages and mid-range resorts, and in the examples reported rooms start at roughly
. Book early in peak season.
Meals are taken at the restaurants and cafés along the village beach. A meal usually costs
or more. There are almost no restaurants near the falls, so bring drinking water and snacks. Port Barton has ATMs, but reportedly they can run out of cash, so bring plenty of cash.

If you stay a day or two in Port Barton, a place near the beach is convenient because it is close to restaurants and tour operators. A simple plan is to visit the falls on the first morning and relax on the beach in the afternoon. Asking the staff at your accommodation to introduce a tricycle driver makes negotiating the fare much easier.
Sign the logbook at the entrance and put a small amount in the donation box. The amount is up to you, usually about
Agree on a round-trip fare with the driver waiting for you before you set off by tricycle.
The unpaved road can turn to mud, so wear trekking shoes or sandals with good grip. Flip-flops may be slippery.
Bring swimwear, a towel, a change of clothes and a waterproof bag, and change out of wet clothes in the hut.
Going early in the morning means fewer people and cooler weather. You can also avoid afternoon showers.
Bring plenty of water and snacks, and take your trash back with you.
Carry enough cash. Donations, transport and meals are all easier with cash.
Ask your operator whether Pamuayan Beach is included in your island-hopping tour and plan around it.
For photos, the rocks in front of the falls show the water stream well. Be careful of slipping when you step on the rocks, and bring a waterproof case for your smartphone.
Rather than walking alone, going with two or three people lets you share the tricycle fare and is safer.
After rain the road turns to mud and the stream can swell dangerously, so check the weather before you go.
The rocks and stepping stones in the stream are mossy and slippery. Cross slowly and do not rush.
According to reviews, there may be leeches in the water, so consider long socks or other protection.
Road works and mud can change how far vehicles can go, so check locally.
Emergency medical care is reportedly limited to a small clinic in Port Barton. Bring your own basic medicines.
The donation, transport fares and operating arrangements may change, so check the latest announcements.
If you drive a motorbike yourself, you can slip easily on unpaved and muddy sections, so use a tricycle if you are inexperienced and always wear a helmet.
The village that serves as your base. Beaches, restaurants and island-hopping operators are all here, and the falls are about

A very long beach on the San Vicente side. It is worth a visit before or after your Port Barton stay.
